comments.body: Historical audit of incremental re-review (lever: carry forward per-criterion verdicts): REJECTED by the data. 894 BLOCK→re-review transitions: 37% block on ≥1 criterion NOT in the original block (18% entirely-new criteria); the most common new criteria (G1G2, G6, E4, COH, E6) are cross-cutting whole-plan criteria that a changed-sections-only design would carry forward. Control: same-material re-runs produce 0% all-new-criteria blocks (15% mixed = nondeterminism floor), so new-criteria blocks on revised material are real revision-induced defects. Skipping unchanged criteria would have missed blocking findings in ~2 of 5 re-reviews. Companion finding: 307/1,457 full-LLM re-reviews (21%) ran on IDENTICAL material fingerprints — 171 triggered by base-sha drift alone — the cleanest remaining quality-neutral savings target. Analysis script + output in reports/llm-gate-cost-2026-08-11/round2/.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body: Round 5 — design questions answered with data. (Q3) BLOCK→PASS flip attribution: 8% of all flips (31/404) happened with NO material change (pure flap); revised-material cited-text attribution is unrecoverable historically (SNAPSHOT compaction dropped old descriptions) — recommend recording cited-anchor hashes in the sidecar going forward. Staged re-review (re-run blocked criteria first) modeled NEGATIVE: 45% of re-reviews PASS and would each pay an extra serial stage-0 call; the mixed bucket (19%) converts one review into two author rounds; only the 13% persisting-only bucket wins — net ≈ break-even before latency, negative after. The DET cited-anchor pre-check captures the same win with zero LLM calls. (Q4) Overlap drain ROI: 0 of 2,093 plan reviews ever surfaced an overlap finding — the drain (~$165/5-days local + its failure storms) is not accomplishing its goal; recommend overlap_drain=off (config kill switch exists) pending redesign, or gate to ticket-creation only. (Q5) Cache TTL cliff CONFIRMED (read-share 68.7% at <5min gaps → 0.0% at >5min) but small: ~5% of consecutive calls are cold ≈ 2-3% recoverable — deprioritize. Analyses in reports/llm-gate-cost-2026-08-11/round2/.

## CloudWatch quantification of the Bedrock error blast radius from the 2026-08-10/11 model-comparison runs

An automated ops error sweep pulled AWS/Bedrock metrics (account 896586841071, us-east-1) for 2026-08-05T00:00Z -> 2026-08-12T04:00Z. Posting the numbers here because the errors are **attributable to the model-comparison experiments run under this ticket**, and because they are now fully explained by [rebar:e800-c107-d4ac-463b] (Nova 10k output ceilings), which has since closed and landed on main as f7e684c300.

**InvocationClientErrors by ModelId — the spike:**

| ModelId | 08-10 21:00 PDT | 08-10 22:00 PDT | 08-11 07:00 PDT |
|---|---|---|---|
| us.amazon.nova-pro-v1:0 | 2 | **50** | **16** |
| us.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0 | - | 6 | - |
| us.amazon.nova-premier-v1:0 | - | 1 | - |
| us.deepseek.r1-v1:0 | - | 2 | - |

Roughly **77 client errors**, ~94% of them on the Nova family, in a two-hour concentration plus one follow-on hour. This matches e800's account precisely: every Nova call riding the raise-to-model-max seam was rejected with `ValidationException: The maximum tokens you requested exceeds the model limit of 10000` before it ran.

**Two things worth carrying forward for the cost analysis:**

1. **The Claude ladder was essentially untouched** — 1-3 client errors each across the whole week for the opus/sonnet/haiku slots. The `rebar-bedrock-invoke-client-errors` alarm is dimensioned on those three slots only, so it correctly stayed OK throughout. That is the alarm behaving as designed, but it also means **a cheap-model experiment can fail wholesale without any alarm noticing** — worth knowing before this ticket recommends routing real gate traffic to a cheap model.
2. **us.deepseek.r1-v1:0 took 2 client errors and is NOT covered by e800's fix**, which added ceilings for nova-pro / nova-2-lite / nova-lite / nova-micro only. If DeepSeek stays in the candidate set for the lever option book, it likely needs its own ceiling entry. Two errors is thin evidence, so treat this as a flag to check rather than a finding.

**Separately, InvocationServerErrors** (5xx, i.e. Bedrock-side not request-side): 1 on 08-05, 1 on 08-07, then **17 clustered on 2026-08-11 10:00-12:00 PDT**. These are not explained by e800 and are not a rebar defect — but a cost/latency model built from that window should know the provider had a bad two hours in it.

For scale: total Invocations peaked at 48,780 on 2026-08-10, so even the worst error hour is a fraction of a percent of traffic.

Reported by an automated ops error sweep; read-only AWS calls, no code changed.

comments.body:
# Why the code-review severity axes are inert — root cause, zero-LLM (2026-08-12)

Operator question before approving Phase 3: *"consider why they're inert before acting on this.
we see very few code review findings."* Answer: **the axes are inert because the block decision
does not read them for 98.5% of findings — not because they are uninformative, and not because
the reviewer finds little.** The ≤0.77% level-collapse flip rate recorded above is a *confounded*
measurement. Corpus: all 1,545 `code_review` sidecar events in the tracker (3,839 findings),
re-scored offline through the shipped `rebar.llm.review_kernel.decide.impact`.

## 1. Distribution headline

| metric | value |
|---|---|
| code-review runs | 1,545 |
| findings | 3,839 — advisory 2,852 / dropped 913 / indeterminate 34 / **blocking 40** |
| verdicts | PASS 1,500 (97.1%) · BLOCK 39 (2.5%) · INDETERMINATE 6 |
| reviews with **0 blocking** | 1,506 / 1,545 = **97.5%** |
| reviews with **0 findings at all** | 470 / 1,545 = 30.4% |
| findings per review | median **2**, mean 2.48 (mode: 0, then 2, then 1) |
| tier | LLM 3,772 · DET 59 |
| **blocking by tier** | **DET 30 · LLM 2 · untiered 8** |

The operator's "0–2 advisory non-blocking" observation is exactly right and is the *normal* mode.
But the reviewer is **not** quiet: it emits 2.48 findings/run and self-labels **183 of them
`major` or `critical`** (159 major + 24 critical). **Every one of those 183 landed in `advisory`
except 2.** The LLM's total contribution to the block decision across the whole corpus is
**2 findings in 1,545 reviews (0.13%)**. Blocking is effectively a *deterministic* gate:
`bugfix-size-attestation` (27) + `sec`/`security` (10) + `secret-detection` (3).

Top advisory criteria: tests 1,399 · maintainability 672 · correctness 617 · edge-cases 415 ·
regression 284 · error-handling 172. Top dropped: docs 328 · tests 169 · maintainability 145.

## 2. Root cause — two structural AND-gates, neither of which is severity

**(i) Blocking is criterion-routed, not severity-routed.** Cross-tab of
`block_threshold` × `blocking_enabled` × `tier`:

```
(0.95, False, LLM)  3353     <- 98.2% of scored findings: blocking DISABLED
(0.54, True,  LLM)    51     <- the ONLY blocking-enabled criterion: `security`
(0.90, False, LLM)    10     <- project.review-phase-boundaries, also disabled
(None, None,  DET)    59     <- deterministic, no axes at all
```

Only `security` (51 findings, 1.3%) is blocking-enabled. For the other 3,363, the severity axes
are graded, serialized, and then discarded — the decision was fixed by routing before `impact()`
was consulted.

**(ii) For those 3,363, the 0.95 threshold is functionally unreachable.** `impact()` is
`(max(prod,debt) + blast + likelihood + reversibility) / 4`, each term ∈ {0.33, 0.67, 1.0}.
Exhaustive enumeration of all 432 attribute combinations:

- **7 / 432 combos (1.6%) reach ≥ 0.95**, and **all 7 require the exact conjunction
  `blast_radius=system` AND `likelihood=high` AND `reversibility=hard`** (plus prod or debt =
  high). The threshold is not a severity dial — it is a hard 3-way AND on the rarest level of
  three axes.
- The next attainable score below 0.95 is **0.9175**. There is a **dead zone**: no finding can
  ever score in (0.9175, 0.95).

Observed marginals over 3,738 graded findings: `blast_radius=system` **92** · `likelihood=high`
**246** · `reversibility=hard` **7** · **all-three conjunction: 0 (zero) occurrences.**

Empirical impact distribution: p50 **0.30**, p90 0.32, p99 0.60, **max 0.90**. Median gap to
threshold **0.65**; only 12 of 3,414 findings land within 0.10 of their threshold. The axes are
never exercised anywhere near the decision boundary because **the boundary is outside the
observed — and nearly outside the attainable — range.**

**(iii) Even the one live path is degenerate.** All 7 findings that ever met their threshold
scored *exactly* 0.54 (= the threshold), and only **2** became blocking: blocking on `security`
additionally requires `validity == 1.0`. Findings at impact 0.54 with validity 0.857 or 0.714
stayed advisory. On that path `impact` behaves as a **binary** (0.54 fires vs ~0.30 doesn't),
and the real discriminator is validity, not the ordinal ladder.

## 3. Hypotheses adjudicated

- **(a) "few findings, mostly advisory — axes never exercised near the threshold"** —
  **TRUE but it is the symptom, not the cause.** Median gap-to-threshold 0.65 confirms the
  non-exercise; §2 explains why it is structural, not a volume artifact. Adding 10x the findings
  would not move it.
- **(b) "threshold/aggregation crushes variance — mean-of-attributes dilution"
  (idea `neat-sooty-termite`)** — **CONFIRMED, and the ticket understates it.** It is not merely
  that the mean dilutes a high-severity axis; it is that mean-of-4 against a 0.95 cut collapses
  the whole 5-axis ordinal space into a 3-way AND satisfied 0 times in 3,738 gradings, with a
  0.9175→0.95 dead zone. **This is the root cause.**
- **(c) "reviewer genuinely finds little (fleet effect: clean changes)"** — **REFUTED as the
  primary cause.** 3,839 findings, 2.48/run, only 30% zero-finding runs, 183 self-labeled
  major/critical. The reviewer finds plenty; what is rare is *blocking*, not *finding*. (A
  fleet effect may well contribute to severity being mostly `minor` — 2,161 of 3,839 — but it
  cannot explain 183 major/critical findings passing.)
- **(d) "reviewer under-reports (prompt/calibration reluctance)"** — **REFUTED for severity
  labelling.** The model applies `critical`/`major` freely and its labels are simply not
  consulted by the gate. The weekly series shows **no reporting decay**: advisory/run runs
  2.91 (W28), 2.07, 1.10, 1.73, 2.01, 2.20 (W33) — stationary, no step-down after any
  calibration/prompt/routing commit. The rise in blocking (W32: 21, W33: 10, vs 0–8 before) is
  fully attributable to the **DET** criteria `secret-detection` and `bugfix-size-attestation`
  first appearing in W32 (commit `1920dc9fe5` "Escalate big bug fixes to real review") — i.e.
  the gate got teeth from *deterministic* checks, not from LLM severity.
  A separate *recall* question remains open (round-2 measured Nova Pro at ~50–57% blocking-
  criteria recall on plan-review), but under-reporting is **not** why the axes are inert.

**Verdict: (b) is the cause; (a) is its symptom; (c) and (d) are refuted as primary.**

## 4. Recommendation on Phase 3 — do NOT proceed as scoped

The migration plan's post-audit note concludes "Phase 3 is UNBLOCKED and LOW-RISK: code-review's
ordinal ladder carries almost no decision weight … so its migration or simplification can
proceed." **That inference does not hold on this evidence.** The ≤0.77% flip rate measures a
ladder wired to a decision that is switched off — it is evidence of *disconnection*, not of
*uninformativeness*. You cannot conclude an instrument is uncalibrated by reading it while it
is unplugged. Migrating ordinals→kind-sets under that measurement would:

1. **Bake in the defect.** A kind-set reconstruction validated against "flips ≤0.77%" is
   validated against a constant function. Any kind set — including a random one — passes.
2. **Spend the change budget on the wrong layer.** The ordinal encoding is not what makes
   code-review pass everything; routing (`blocking_enabled=False` on 98.2%) and an unreachable
   0.95 cut are.
3. **Make the real defect harder to see later**, by rewriting the very fields that currently
   document it.

**Sequence instead:**

- **P3.0 (zero-LLM, do first) — fix the threshold/aggregation, then re-measure.** Either lower
  the non-security cut into the attainable range (the corpus p99 is 0.60; the 0.9175 ceiling
  means anything above ~0.92 is a no-op), or replace mean-of-4 with a max/floor rule so one
  `high`+`system` axis is not averaged away by three `easy`/`local` ones. Decide separately
  and deliberately **which criteria should be blocking-enabled** — today it is exactly one.
  This is a policy question for the operator, not a modelling one.
- **P3.1 — re-run `code_decisiveness.py` against the corrected decision rule.** Only then does
  the flip rate mean anything. If the axes still flip <1% *with a live threshold*, the
  ordinal→kind-set migration is justified and cheap. If they flip materially, Phase 2's
  "reconstruct levels deterministically" discipline applies here too.
- **Phase 3 as currently written: hold.** Not "pointless" — **premature and, on the current
  justification, actively wrong.**

Cheap intermediate sanity check, zero-LLM: replay the 183 existing `major`/`critical` LLM
findings through a candidate decision rule and inspect how many *should* have blocked. No new
inference calls; the findings and their axes are already recorded.

## 5. If you still want an under-reporting probe (not needed for Phase 3)

Under-reporting is refuted for *labelling*, but *recall* is untested for code-review. Cheapest
confirmation: replay N historically-defective changes through `review-code` and count catches.
Sourcing gold: commits that were later reverted, or whose ticket has a `discovered_from` child
filed as a bug against them. At the measured **$1.42/run** code-review cost, **N=20 ≈ $28**,
**N=30 ≈ $43** (single epoch; double for 2-epoch stability). Recommend **N=20, one epoch, ~$28**
— and only *after* P3.0, since a recall probe against a gate that cannot block measures the
finder in isolation and tells you nothing about the gate. **Not run; approval required.**

*(Analysis-only. Zero LLM calls. Scripts are ad-hoc re-scores through the shipped `impact()`;
method matches round2/code_decisiveness.py with the field-shape correction applied.)*

DEPRECATION REMOVAL-READINESS SURVEY (2026-08-12) — analysis only, no code change, no claim.

Scope: "what was deprecated in prior releases that we can now remove?" Surveyed rebar._deprecations (the central registry), docs/ + CHANGELOG.md + docs/release-notes.md + docs/api-stability.md + docs/migrations.md, ADR 0050, the tracker, and live origin/tickets store data (81,840 commits; 1,884 active SNAPSHOT blobs audited).

== HEADLINE ==
NOTHING with a recorded removal condition has met it. rebar is at 0.11.0 (tag v0.11.0, 2026-08-06); EVERY scheduled deprecation in the registry carries remove_in="v1.0.0" (_deprecations.py:47, _MAJOR), and v1.0.0 has not shipped. docs/api-stability.md:30 adds an independent floor: an alias survives at least one minor release AFTER its replacement ships. The two headline candidates shipped their deprecation IN v0.11.0, six days ago, so even that minimum floor is unmet — earliest legal removal is v0.12.0.

The one real lever is precedent, not schedule: docs/release-notes.md:226 and :249 record TWO completed "pre-1.0 breaking" passes (DE7, and ticket 5899's sibling pass) that removed scheduled shims EARLY, by operator ruling rather than at v1.0.0. So the actionable question for the operator is not "which deprecations expired?" (none) but "do we open a third pre-1.0 breaking window, and what goes in it?"

== TIER 1 — READY TO REMOVE NOW (no policy conflict) ==

1. The retired .gitattributes migration arm. src/rebar/_commands/init.py:600-616 + _RETIRED_GITATTRIBUTES_LINES at init.py:69 strips the retired ".reconciler-* merge=ours" line. Introduced bbfa1c1d9b (2026-07-05). This store ALREADY ran it: git log origin/tickets -- .gitattributes shows exactly two commits, the second being 826d5ae379 "drop retired .reconciler-* merge=ours"; the live blob contains only ".bridge_state/* merge=ours". The arm is permanently unreachable here.
   Size: ~15 LOC, one file. Risk: LOW but not zero — it is a convergence unit, so it still matters for any clone that has not swept since 2026-07-05. Verdict: READY, conditional on confirming no unswept pre-2026-07-05 clone. This is the only genuinely expired, genuinely dead thing found.

== TIER 2 — REMOVABLE ONLY IN A NEW PRE-1.0 BREAKING WINDOW (operator call) ==

2. The single-pass review surfaces (story 316a, alias common-middle-yearling, CLOSED). Three registry rows, _deprecations.py:112-114: CLI "rebar review", lib "rebar.llm.review_ticket", MCP "review_ticket". Deprecated 31f352d535 (2026-08-04); shipped in v0.11.0 (CHANGELOG.md:128-129 "The deprecated single-pass rebar review operation was retired in favor of review-plan, verify-completion, and review-code"). Recorded condition: remove_in=v1.0.0; docs/cli-reference.md:557 states "Deprecated (story 316a; removal in v1.0.0)".
   IMPORTANT SCOPING FINDING: this is much smaller than it looks. The single-pass ENGINE _review_ticket_impl must STAY — it has three live internal consumers: src/rebar/_mcp_llm.py:92-95, src/rebar/llm/review_workflows.py:86, src/rebar/llm/evals/eval_solver.py:348. So removal deletes only three thin public entry points (the warn-and-delegate wrapper at llm/operations.py:135-183, the CLI intercept at _cli/__init__.py:513 + _llm_commands.py:133, and the MCP tool at _mcp_llm.py:61). schemas/review_result.schema.json also STAYS (still the engine's output contract).
   Size: MODERATE — 42 non-impl refs in src, 24 in docs, 19 test files. Risk: LOW internally; the only real exposure is an external importer of rebar.llm.review_ticket, which is exactly why 316a chose announce-then-remove.
   Verdict: NOT YET on policy (deprecation is 8 days old and shipped in the current release). Strongest candidate for the next breaking window.

3. REBAR_LLM_MODEL / llm.model. _deprecations.py:101, deprecated 1fbfb5c691 (2026-08-01), also in v0.11.0. A SUPERSESSION (not a rename) by the [tool.rebar.llm.model_classes] slots, which landed 2026-07-31 (4559258b98). Condition recorded by the parent story (eb58, alias fiendish-communal-cuttlefish, CLOSED): "DEPRECATED with a migration window rather than kept as a permanent alias", remove_in=v1.0.0. docs/env-vars.md:66 and docs/config.md:317 both state the window.
   Size: SMALL (one registry row, the alias resolver in config.py, llm/config.py, llm/model_classes.py). Risk: LOW.
   Verdict: NOT YET — 11 days old, shipped in the current release. Second candidate for the window.

== TIER 3 — NOT YET, BLOCKED ON A NAMED CONDITION ==

4. The resolved_statuses keys. Deprecation landed TODAY (72a57c30ab / 77cdff2cdd, 2026-08-12). CRITICAL DISTINCTION — there are TWO keys and only one is inert:
   - reconciler.resolved_statuses (_config_schema.py:465) is LIVE, read by the Jira Data Center adapter (adapters/jira_datacenter/settings.py:101 -> backend.py:303). NOT a removal candidate. The "inert" language in docs/user-guide.md:498 does NOT apply to it.
   - jira.resolved_statuses (_config_schema.py:490) is the inert one; its only consumer (adapters/jira/probe.py) was deleted with the dormant inbound absence-probe port (task f020, commit b95c097fd4 2026-08-12).
   Decision ticket restful-chaseable-macaw (549c-032f-6cb0-4258, task, in_progress): "DECISION: deprecate (option 1), do NOT remove now". Hard-removal follow-up salted-growable-murrelet (f408-64ad-ee41-46b6, task, open) is "deliberately BLOCKED ON OPERATOR SIGN-OFF", first AC "operator sign-off for the removal is recorded on this ticket" — unchecked, ticket has zero comments.
   Verdict: NOT YET — approval-gated AND release-gated, deprecated hours ago.

5. fastmcp / mcp 2.0 (epic bared-nickel-insect, 732b-51df-acf2-477b, status idea). Correcting the premise: the standalone fastmcp package is NOT a dependency at all. rebar uses the BUNDLED mcp.server.fastmcp from the official SDK, pinned mcp>=1.28.1,<2 (uv.lock resolves 1.29.0), and only as the optional [mcp] extra. It is not deprecated in-repo — the opposite: ADR 0050 (docs/adr/0050-mcp-optional-auth-resource-server.md:25-30) explicitly evaluated and REJECTED the standalone fastmcp auth stack ("semver-exempt and has its own CVE history"). That is a recent Accepted decision, not drift.
   Real risk to record: in mcp 2.0.0 the mcp.server.fastmcp path is REMOVED (FastMCP renamed to MCPServer under mcp.server.mcpserver). The <2 cap fences it off today, but all six import sites (mcp_server.py:578, scripts/gen_mcp_reference.py:79, and 4 tests) are hard blockers for a future 2.x bump.
   Ticket's recorded condition: "stay on mcp>=1.28.1,<2 for now; execute this ticket once mcp 2.0.x has a patch release or two rather than migrating on a .0" (2.0.0 shipped 2026-07-28).
   Verdict: NOT YET — upstream-maturity gated, and nothing here is a removal anyway; it is a forward migration.

6. Event-schema / reducer compat folds — NOT REMOVABLE, essentially permanently. Audited all 1,884 active snapshot blobs. Live old shapes persist in immutable history:
   - creation_channel re-inference (_processors.py:756-769, :147-175): 1,118 / 1,884 active snapshots hold creation_channel "unknown". Very hot.
   - FILE_IMPACT tri-state (_processors.py:689-694): 265 / 1,884 lack file_impact_scope.
   - plan_review_phase bootstrap (_processors.py:696-709): 155 / 1,884 lack it.
   - Legacy-Jira envelope fingerprint (_version.py:146-147): the only provenance signal for pre-2026-07-17 Jira imports.
   - 19-digit-ns filename ordering (_store/hlc.py:20-23, reducer/_sort.py:4): the earliest live event filename is 1780980854246350000-..., so every pre-2026-06-17 name is that shape. Permanent.
   - frame_key -> step_id fallback, EDIT.tags whole-field handling: v1 events are immutable.
   These read append-only git blobs on origin/tickets that will never be rewritten; and compaction deliberately never deletes a superseded SNAPSHOT (.retired is retained, docs/event-schema.md:159-161, _replay.py:191), so old-shape snapshots persist regardless. Removing any of these would silently mis-project ~1,100 tickets. Verdict: NOT REMOVABLE.
   One narrow exception worth naming: the attestations fold-in inner body (_processors.py:727-735, duplicated at reducer/_cache.py:99-106) is COLD — 588 snapshots enter the branch but ZERO carry a signature dict to fold, because task 352b hardcoded the mirror-strip in compact.py. docs/migrations.md:257-260 already anticipates this and deliberately KEEPS it: safe to remove "only once no snapshot predating the attestations map remains in ANY store" — unverifiable for foreign clones. Verdict: NOT YET, and cheap to keep.

7. Ensure-registry: NO retirable migration shims. Six units (env-id, gc-config, merge-ours, gitattributes, gitignore, store-compat). It is School B — convergent desired-state, no version ledger (docs/migrations.md:10-13) — so "target state is now universal" means a unit reports ok, NOT that it is deletable. env-id / gc-config / merge-ours write per-clone local state and can never be no-ops. Only the gitattributes strip ARM is dead (item 1 above).

== TIER 4 — NEEDS OPERATOR DECISION (deprecated by policy, no recorded condition) ==

8. 4-digit / two-quad short-ID acceptance (_ids.py:53 _SHORT_ID_RE, resolution at :256). Operator policy is "aliases preferred, don't break, don't advertise" — there is NO registry row, NO removal condition, and no tracker ticket (searched: "short id", "4-digit"). Usage evidence: all 60 most-recent commit trailers use the FULL 19-char canonical id; zero short-form; 1 of 40 recent subjects used a 4-hex prefix. So the path is effectively unexercised in identity-sensitive artifacts but remains a convenience input for CLI resolution. Verdict: NEEDS OPERATOR DECISION — removing it is a user-visible input break with no announced window, which would contradict the announce-then-remove precedent.

9. Undocumented CLI compat aliases with no registry row and no window: verify-authorship (back-compat alias for verify-identity, _cli/__init__.py:565, documented in docs/exit-codes.md:191) and bridge-status (hidden alias, _cli/__init__.py:121-122, docs/user-guide.md:394). Neither is registered, so neither has a scheduled removal. Verdict: NEEDS OPERATOR DECISION — if we want these gone they must first be REGISTERED and announced, not silently deleted.

== EXPLICIT NON-CANDIDATES (do not remove) ==
- The 8 PERMANENT registry rows (_deprecations.py:81-91): REBAR_NO_SYNC, COMPACT_THRESHOLD, SCRATCH_BASE_DIR, REBAR_ACLI_TIMEOUT, RECONCILER_ABSENT_GET_BUDGET, REBAR_ID_GUARD_MODE, REBAR_VERIFY_OVERLAP_ENABLED, verify.overlap_enabled. These are ergonomic RENAMES kept forever by design; removing them buys nothing.
- The tombstone registry (_deprecations.py:203-236): already-removed inputs kept as fail-loud migration errors. Deleting a tombstone would re-silence a removed load-bearing input. Keep.
- _store/compat.py: FORWARD-compat (refuses to mutate a store written by a newer binary). Not backward-compat cruft.
- reducer forward-compat unknown-event skip (_replay.py:188-195): protects against newer clones. Structural.

== REGISTRY HYGIENE (a positive finding) ==
The deprecation registry is complete and trustworthy. warn_deprecated raises KeyError on an unregistered surface, and tests/unit/test_deprecation_registry.py source-scans for raw emissions bypassing it. Independent verification: the only warnings.warn in src/rebar outside _deprecations.py is llm/prompting/prompts_frontmatter.py:172, which is an unknown-frontmatter-key warning, not a deprecation. docs/env-vars.md (generated) likewise lists exactly one deprecated env with a window. So this survey's registry-derived inventory can be treated as exhaustive for signalled surfaces.

== RECOMMENDATION ==
Remove now: item 1 only (tiny). Everything else is a scheduling decision. If the operator wants to bank the cleanup, the cheapest high-value move is to open a third pre-1.0 breaking window at v0.12.0 carrying items 2 and 3 together (both are v1.0.0-scheduled supersessions, both are small once you know _review_ticket_impl stays, and both would then satisfy the one-minor-release floor). Items 4-7 should not be touched; items 8-9 need an announce step before they are removable at all.

The reason-scoped counters were brand new, so their first run computed new = total = all retained history. The helper already clamps the OPPOSITE direction (negative delta / lost history, per bug 2dc7-31b7-ecbb-4cd2 and the 1648 rotation double-count clamp); the cold-start case (offset ABSENT rather than journal SHRUNK) is the complementary gap and is unguarded.

Under the usual terraform-then-deploy order both 1-datapoint latches would have fired instantly off stale history — including the signal-unavailable alarm, whose own description calls it 'the URGENT one ... EVERY deploy is running blind', from a single already-resolved 2026-08-04 event.
Classified FALSE-POSITIVE-GENERATING metric defect, not an alarm-threshold problem: the alarm predicate is right to fire on a nonzero count, the count was fabricated. Every one of them was a review that finished (or would have) shortly after the deferral budget expired. ## Context
Analysis-only record of LLM gate economics since the Bedrock switch. No production or repository code change is part of this ticket. The work measured per-gate and per-ticket cost, evaluated quality-neutral and model-swap levers, ran cheap-model experiments, and produced a phased ordinal-to-binary migration plan.

## Durable deliverables
- Existing ticket comments record experiment rounds 1 through 6, costs, gold-set outcomes, rejected levers, and follow-up tickets.
- The full report is published at https://claude.ai/code/artifact/725e8b52-688d-49ed-a286-4571bedce34d.
- The comment marked ORDINAL_MIGRATION_PLAN_DURABLE_COPY records the phased migration plan and its validation/approval boundaries.
- Local research files under reports/llm-gate-cost-2026-08-11 are intentionally gitignored working artifacts, not committed deliverables and not closure evidence.

## Results
Plan review measured mean 3.02 dollars per run, code review 1.42 dollars, completion verification 2.24 dollars, and mean 11.85 dollars per completed ticket. The experiments rejected Haiku for agentic review, rejected per-criterion re-review after the historical audit, retained Sonnet for completion verification, and identified bounded Nova pilots and terminal-failure fixes as the credible next levers. Execution of any migration remains separate work requiring operator approval.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] Cost analysis and per-gate/per-ticket figures are durably recorded. Verify: `rebar show childsafe-bizarre-lorikeet | grep -F "cost per ticket COMPLETED"` exits 0.
- [x] Cheap-model experiment outputs and dispositions are durably recorded. Verify: `rebar show childsafe-bizarre-lorikeet | grep -F "Follow-up experiments complete"` exits 0.
- [x] The ordinal-migration plan is durably recorded without executing the migration. Verify: `rebar show childsafe-bizarre-lorikeet | grep -F "ORDINAL_MIGRATION_PLAN_DURABLE_COPY"` exits 0.

## File impact
None. This is an analysis record; evidence lives in the shared ticket history and published artifact.
